title: Why It’s Okay To Let Your Students Experience Failure e-failure/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin challenges the reflex among caring teachers to soften failure for students, arguing that repeatedly downplaying poor test scores or behavior lapses robs students of critical life lessons. He contends students are 'far better off' being allowed to genuinely feel disappointment, since that discomfort is what drives real change; artificially inflating grades or minimizing setbacks is not only dishonest but harmful. This doesn't mean withholding encouragement altogether—rather, praise should be offered truthfully and only after students have had the dignity of experiencing their actual results. He frames childhood as the ideal, low-stakes time to build the resilience needed for future setbacks like rejection or job loss, positioning honest accountability as an act of love that prepares students for adulthood.
points: Teachers habitually soften students' failures out of genuine care, but this conditioning prevents critical life lessons from being learned.
Students are better off feeling real disappointment—'these churning, sinking, aching feelings'—because that discomfort drives lasting change.
Giving a 'meaningless C when they deserve an F' is dishonest and harmful, not kind.
Encouragement and praise still have a place, but should be offered truthfully, after students have experienced the reality of their performance.
Childhood, when stakes are low, is the ideal time to build the resilience needed to face future rejection, job loss, or hardship.
quotes: The truth is, our students are far better off when allowed to experience their mistakes, failures, and defeats.
We do our students a disservice by interfering with the normal, human, and energy-producing powers of regret.
We owe it to our students not to minimize failure, but to allow them to feel it.
A meaningless ‘C’ when they deserve an ‘F’ is not only dishonest, but it’s harmful.
Now is the time, when the stakes are low, to build the fortitude needed to overcome that closed door, that letter of rejection, that loss of job.
They need to experience failure now, in the safety of your loving guidance, so that it doesn’t crush them in the future.
